item.title: “Monks, a jackal saw a tortoise from afar and approached it. Having approached, it stood to one side and thought: ‘When this tortoise stretches out…
item.description:
“Monks, a jackal saw a tortoise from afar and approached it. Having approached, it stood to one side and thought: ‘When this tortoise stretches out any of its limbs or its neck, I will seize it right there, break it, and eat it.’ But, monks, because the tortoise did not stretch out any limb or its neck, the jackal became disenchanted with the tortoise and left, not having gained an opportunity. So too, monks, Māra constantly and relentlessly stands in ambush for you, thinking: ‘Perhaps I can gain an opportunity through the eye … through the tongue … through the mind.’ Therefore, monks, guard the sense faculties. When you see a form with the eye, do not grasp the general feature, do not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — restrain that cause, guard the eye, practice restraint of the eye. When you hear a sound … smell an odor … taste a flavor … feel a touch … cognize a phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp the general feature, do not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — restrain that cause, guard the mind, practice restraint of the mind. Monks, when you live guarding the sense faculties, Māra will become disenchanted with you and leave, not gaining an opportunity, just like the jackal with the tortoise.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.240

item.title: Elder Nun Abhayā: O fearless nun! This body is so fragile — Worldlings here, Delighting, are often lustful. I will abandon this body, Mindful and…
item.description:
Elder Nun Abhayā:

O fearless nun!
This body is so fragile —
Worldlings here,
Delighting, are often lustful.
I will abandon this body,
Mindful and clearly comprehending.

Without heedlessness, I will strive,
I will strive to escape the painful state.
With craving destroyed, I have attained —
Accomplishing the Buddha’s teaching.

From: Therīgāthā 2.9
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these three feelings. What three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Pleasant feeling, monks, should be seen as suffering. Painful feeling should…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three feelings. What three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Pleasant feeling, monks, should be seen as suffering. Painful feeling should be seen as a dart. Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling should be seen as impermanent. When, monks, a monk sees pleasant feeling as suffering, sees painful feeling as a dart, sees neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent — then, monks, he is called a monk who has right view, who has cut off craving, who has destroyed the fetters. By thoroughly breaking through conceit, he has made an end of suffering.

One who sees pleasure as suffering,
And sees pain as a dart,
Sees the neutral feeling
As impermanent —
That monk sees rightly,
Fully understanding feelings.

Having fully understood feelings,
He is defilement-free in this very life.
At the breaking of the body, that Dhamma-abider,
The great sage, is beyond measure.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 36.5

item.title: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are tied, infatuated, utterly committed to these five strands of sensual pleasure, who do not see their peril, who…
item.description:
“Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are tied, infatuated, utterly committed to these five strands of sensual pleasure, who do not see their peril, who do not know the escape from them, and who enjoy them—they should be understood as having fallen into misfortune, into calamity, and are being used by Māra as he wishes. Monks, just as a forest deer that has fallen into a trap must lie down—that deer should be understood as having fallen into misfortune, into calamity, and is being used by the hunter as he wishes. When the hunter comes, the deer cannot leave as it wishes. So too, monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are tied … are being used by Māra as he wishes.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta

item.title: “Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I thought: ‘The five strands of sensual pleasure that this mind…
item.description:
“Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I thought: ‘The five strands of sensual pleasure that this mind formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — regarding them, my mind becomes inflamed when they are present, and diminishes when they are future, not yet attained.’ Then, monks, I thought: ‘The five strands of sensual pleasure that this mind formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — regarding them, for my own benefit, I will dwell heedful, protecting my mind with mindfulness.’ Therefore, monks, regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure that your minds formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — your minds become inflamed when they are present, and diminish when they are future, not yet attained. Therefore, monks, regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure that your minds formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — for your own benefit, dwell heedful, protecting your minds with mindfulness.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.117

item.title: Māra: You are young and beautiful, I am young and in my prime. With the five-tuned lute, Enjoy yourself, Khemā. Elder Nun Khemā: With this…
item.description:
Māra:

You are young and beautiful,
I am young and in my prime.
With the five-tuned lute,
Enjoy yourself, Khemā.

Elder Nun Khemā:

With this foul body,
Diseased and fragile —
I am disenchanted, disgusted.
Sensual desire has been uprooted.

Sensual desires are like swords and spears —
The aggregates are a chopping block.
What you call sensual pleasure —
I have now abandoned it.

Everywhere, delight is destroyed,
The mass of delusion is shattered.
Know this, O Evil One —
You are defeated, Māra.

You worship the stars!
You worship fire in the deep forest —
You do not know the truth —
Fools think it is pure.

But I pay homage
To the Awakened One, the Supreme Man,
Who has escaped all suffering,
Following the Teacher’s instruction.

From: Therīgāthā 6.3
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Standing to one side, the deity Candana recited this verse to the Blessed One: How can one cross the flood, Steadfast and persevering day and…
item.description:
Standing to one side, the deity Candana recited this verse to the Blessed One:
How can one cross the flood,
Steadfast and persevering day and night?
Without stalling, without clinging —
Who does not sink in the abyss?

(The Blessed One):
One who always has virtue,
Wisdom, and is well-concentrated,
With aroused energy and strength —
That one crosses the hard-to-cross flood.
One who has abandoned perception of lust,
Who has crossed beyond the fetter of form,
Who has destroyed delight and craving for existence —
That one does not sink in the abyss.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.15
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, how does a monk live as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island,…
item.description:
“Monks, how does a monk live as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, seeking no other refuge? Monks, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body internally, ardent, diligent, mindful, clearly comprehending, to remove covetousness and sorrow in the world; abides contemplating feelings as feelings … mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena, ardent, diligent, mindful, clearly comprehending, to remove covetousness and sorrow in the world. Thus, monks, a monk lives as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, seeking no other refuge.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 26 – Cakkavattisutta

item.title: “Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because he…
item.description:
“Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because he sees this body composed of the four great elements increasing and decreasing, being taken up and discarded. Therefore, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding it. But regarding that which is called mind, intellect, consciousness — here, an untaught ordinary person is not capable of disenchantment, not capable of dispassion, not capable of liberation. Why is that? For a long time, monks, an untaught ordinary person has been attached, regarded as ‘mine,’ grasped at: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ Therefore, he is not capable of disenchantment, dispassion, or liberation regarding it.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.61

item.title: “And when, monks, the mind is freed from these five defilements — sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt — then it…
item.description:
“And when, monks, the mind is freed from these five defilements — sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt — then it becomes malleable, wieldy, radiant, not brittle, properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. Regarding whatever state is to be directly known, the mind inclines to direct knowledge, and in each case he attains the ability and capacity to realize that state.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.23
